sb_prompt: DISCUSS GUN CONTROL.  WHERE DO YOU AND THE OTHER CALLER STAND ON A SCALE FROM 1 TO 10
turns: So, I'm an electrician and I've always been into that stuff, but honestly, I just kind of picked it up years ago without really knowing why, and now I'm trying to figure out where I stand on this gun control thing. Where are you on that scale?
I'm a bank teller and I'm pretty skeptical, mostly because my cousin was a cop who lost his life to it.
Oh man, that's so heavy. I get why you're skeptical, honestly.
I don't see why we should take guns away if it puts people at risk.
Yeah, I mean, when you see someone actually getting hurt, it makes you wonder if there's a better way to keep people safe.
You? Did your family ever try to get a gun before?
No, never even thought about it.
No, my family never really talked about it, though I guess my cousin's job made it feel like a big deal around here.
Yeah, I guess I don't really see how that connects to what I do on a job site.
So, do you ever think about it when you're out wiring houses or talking to people?
Yeah, mostly just people coming to fix stuff and getting nervous about who's walking in the door.
Yeah, that actually hits pretty close to home for me too.
Yeah, it's just that kind of fear that makes you think maybe a stricter rule would help calm things down.
I mean, if we lock up every single house, does that actually stop the bad guys from coming in?
That's a fair point, but sometimes it's not even about getting in, it's just about making sure people don't have the tools to cause the damage once they're already inside.
Yeah, but how do you even get a key in a house that's not yours to open without breaking the lock first?
Exactly, you can't lock them out of your own house if they already have a key, so you might as well make sure the people walking around the neighborhood don't have those keys in the first place.
Yeah, but that assumes everyone just walks up with a key, right? Don't people actually buy them?

Exactly, people buy them, and honestly, knowing how to pick a lock or bypass a deadbolt is a skill I teach in school, so I see the danger in just handing them the tools to break into the house in the first place.
Yeah, but what if someone needs it to protect themselves from a burglar?
That's fair, but honestly, if you can't trust the guy next door not to turn that protection around on you, maybe having it in the first place is what makes the whole situation worse.
You think the neighbors are the ones carrying? That sounds like a pretty dark neighborhood if the people next door are the problem.
Yeah, mostly people who've done time or are just looking for a reason to feel tough, and once that happens, it gets hard to stop the stuff that goes down.
Yeah, so if you're talking to folks who've done time, I guess the whole neighborhood dynamic changes pretty fast, right?
Yeah, once you start looking at it that way, it's not just about locking doors anymore, it's about who you let into your own living room.

Yeah, I guess once you start looking at it that way, locking doors feels like just throwing up a wall to keep people out, but if the person inside is the one holding the weapon, the wall doesn't stop them from hurting someone.
Yeah, that's the thing, you can't trust the person inside to not turn the wall into a weapon themselves.
That's a scary way to look at it, but does that mean you're saying strict control is the only way to stop people from having power?
Yeah, mostly, if you can't control who's got power, then locking the doors is just playing defense against someone who's already inside.
So if we take that power away, what's the person inside supposed to do when the door gets kicked in?
That's where it gets tricky, because if you take away the ability to fight back, you're just leaving them completely exposed when the door finally kicks open.
So if they can't defend themselves, who's supposed to call the cops fast enough when the door gets kicked in?
Depends, because if the cops are too slow, then taking the weapon away just means you're the only one who can't stop it from happening.
So you're saying if you don't have the gun, you're basically just waiting for the cops to arrive while someone is already in your room?
Yeah, basically that's the point, because those few seconds of waiting are often all it takes for someone to get hurt before help even shows up.
So if they're already in the room with you, does that mean waiting for the cops is basically just waiting for it to be too late?
Yeah, exactly, that split second is often all it takes before help shows up.
Yeah, but what happens when the person doing the kicking doesn't just want to break in, they want to make sure nobody can ever leave the room at all?
Yeah, that's the part where it gets really scary, because then you're not just locked in, you're trapped with someone who's already decided you don't deserve to be there.
Yeah, but what if they never let you make a move to start with?
